reading.body:
DFW17 publishes 100,000 square feet of technical space but no megawatt figure, making it impossible to assess its compute capacity relative to AI workloads or rank it among Texas facilities that do disclose power.

The floor area alone establishes that this is a substantial, purpose-built facility rather than an edge node, but translating square footage into rack count or accelerator density would require assuming both power density and an undisclosed power figure. Any such estimate would be too speculative to state. What matters for AI scaling is the megawatt ceiling, not the floor.

The four certifications define the compliance envelope. PCI DSS qualifies the site to host payment-card data. ISO 27001 qualifies it for workloads requiring a certified information security management system, which is common among enterprise and government AI tenants with data-governance obligations. ISO 9001 certifies the operator's quality management processes. LEED certifies energy and environmental design. None directly indicate AI training density or high-performance compute readiness.

Texas has 133 mapped data center facilities, of which only 13 publish megawatt figures, totaling 389 MW of disclosed IT capacity. DFW17 is not among those 13 and contributes no published power data to the state total. Without it, the actual compute capacity in the Dallas-Fort Worth metro remains partially hidden.
